subject: dark planet
title: What If a Planet Had No Sun at All? Trillions Don't

scenes.text: What if a planet had no sun at all? Trillions don't, and some might still have oceans.
NASA estimates rogue planets outnumber star-bound worlds about six to one. Most were flung out of young planetary systems.
Lose your star and sunlight vanishes. Heat from the core alone would warm the surface to only about 30 degrees above absolute zero.
But in 1999, Caltech's David Stevenson showed a thick hydrogen atmosphere could trap that heat. The surface could stay near Earth's temperature, with oceans.
The closest probable rogue world, WISE 0855, drifts about 7 light-years away. NASA's Roman telescope could find around 400 Earth-mass ones.
Pitch black forever, no sunrise, and maybe a warm sea. Life might not need a star at all.

description:
What if a planet had no star? Billions to trillions of rogue planets drift through the Milky Way; NASA estimates they outnumber planets orbiting stars by about six to one, most of them thrown out of their systems while young.
Without a sun, core heat alone would leave a surface near 30 kelvin, but a thick hydrogen atmosphere could trap enough heat for liquid oceans, as Caltech's David Stevenson proposed in 1999. NASA's Roman telescope could find around 400 Earth-mass rogue worlds.
What should we run through next?

first_comment: Rogue planets may also form on their own from collapsing gas clouds, like failed stars. Would you rather live on a world with no sun, or one with two?
